messages.body_plain:
Hello INLA team,

I am attempting to do a sensitivity analysis on priors for an SPDE model, but I'm having trouble interpreting the posterior hyperparameters from a model using default priors (i.e., inla.spde2.matern() ). I'm also unsure how to choose range and variance parameters to use in inla.spde2.pcmatern(). What would constitute a non-informative prior?

Thank you!
Pascale

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Choosing range and variance priors for SPDE
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Choosing range and variance priors for SPDE
messages.body_plain:
Hi Pascale,

The default priors in inla.spde2.matern are just that; "default". They only exist to make it easy to run simple tests. Any actual data analysis should set the priors to more sensible values for the problem at hand. The 2015 Lindgren&Rue JSS paper presented one way of doing that, but for all new analysis (with the exception of some nonstationary models) I strongly recommend using inla.spde2.pcmatern() instead, since
the pc-priors tend to be much nicer to work with. Check the Fuglstad et al paper on pc-priors for matern models for more information. The help text for inla.spde2.pcmatern has the reference, and also text about the priors

Practically speaking, there isn't really such a thing as non-informative priors (e.g. flat priors can be highly informative), but the pc-priors for spde model come close, in the sense that they don't impose strong constraints on the parameters, but at the same time tend to stabilise the inference. That said, it's still important to consider the prior parameter settings in the context of the problem.
For example, reasonable values for sigma tend to be very different for "additive Gaussian noise" observations, than for fields in log-linear predictors, since the standard deviation on the log-scale has such an important effect on the nonlinear predictor variability.

Finn

the periodicity is 5 years?

Sincerely,

Rustam

messages.body_plain:
you can check the example in

	inla.doc("seasonal")

the period is related to the indexing set, which is easiest defined as
integers, like 1,2,3...

the season.length=5 is that is the cycle length.

The easiest way to check that you got it right, it to simulate some easy
to estimate data, and check that you get it back and all is looking
good.

see also the GMRF-book at the end of chapter 3.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How does inla.mesh.1d bin time between knots
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How does inla.mesh.1d bin time between knots
messages.body_plain:
By default, inla.mesh.1d defines a piecewise linear basis system, so it does not "group" the time points. Instead, it defines a piecewise linear function with nodes at the input "loc" values (or "knots").
So in your example, 2000 will be mapped to the first node, 2001 will be mapped to 2/3 times the first node value plus 1/3 times the second node value, etc.

Finn

messages.subject: Question about modeling categorical variables in INLA
messages.subject_clean: Question about modeling categorical variables in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have begun working with a new dataset in R-INLA and have two covariates in my model that are categorical variables, including age (adult and yearling) and sex (male and female).

I am using inla.stack and the inla formula as follows:

StackEst <- inla.stack(data = list(y=data$Result),

A = list(A_point, 1),

effects = list(c(s.index, list(Intercept = 1)),
list(Sex = data$sex,
       Age = data$age)),
tag = "Est")

formula < y ~ -1 +  Sex + Age + f(spatial.field2, model = spde1)

When I run the above formula and view the summary of results, inla removes one level for sex, but retains both for age.

I have tried using the expand.factor.strategy = "inla" and assigning one of the levels of the variables to NA, but then I received an error in contrasts message saying that contrasts can only be applied to factors with 2 or more levels.

I have tried the following formula to account for the categorical variables and it runs no problem.

formula < y ~ -1 + f(Sex, model = "iid",  constr = T) + f(Age, model = "iid",  constr = T)  + f(spatial.field2, model = spde1)

Question:
Is accounting for the categorical variables by using (model="iid", constr = T), the best option in this situation, or is there a way to run the model by having one of the levels of each of the categorical variables removed?

Thanks,

Kristin

messages.body_plain:
I would suggest turning your binary factors into binary 0/1 indicator variables instead, since you say you only want to keep one of the two levels from each.
Making explicit 0/1 is the simplest way to control that.

You also need to add + Intercept to your formula if you want to include it in the model (you have it in the stack).

> > list(Sex = data$sex,

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] unexpected intra-variant variances estimation in disaggregation spatial regression model using INLA()
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] unexpected intra-variant variances estimation in disaggregation spatial regression model using INLA()
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your explanation! From multiple infill asymptotics simulations (100 realizations), I found there is a strong correlation between the marginal variances and the kappa estimates of those posterior estimates for the spde representation of the Matern field model from those 100 realizations. Based on this, I have two questions:

(1) Is it appropriate to derive a relationship between those two model parameters (marginal variance and kappa/range) from the simulation data and apply the derived relationship in the real-world data to improve the prediction accuracy in the real-world data scenario? If it is doable, is there a way to constrain the model parameters and apply the derived relationship between the parameters in the inla() model to improve the prediction accuracy in the real-world data scenario?

(2) Or the correlation and the uncertainty estimates of the spde Matern model parameters will not affect the prediction performance of the model with single realization data no matter what constrain/relationship of the model parameters are applied in the model? Since our main goal in the real-world data is to predict the missing values with only one observation and not to estimate the underlying model parameters, this could be helpful. Thanks!!

Bowen

On Monday, January 3, 2022 at 1:15:12 PM UTC-6 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> Like I explained before, this is a fundamental property of even the simplest Gaussian Matern random field model, and has very little specific to do with either inla or the spde representations for Matern fields. Even in the case of a directly observed field (I.e. with no observation noise), infill asymptotics aren’t enough to consistently estimate all the model parameters. The best one can hope for is that the parameter estimates are reasonable, and that the resulting field properties (e.g. spatial prediction/infill) produces appropriate results with appropriate uncertainty estimates. One reference about the non-consistency of parameter estimates is  https://www.jstor.org/stable/20441245
> Non-consistency however doesn’t mean that the parameter estimates are _necessarily_ far from the true values. It just means that there is no guarantee that they will be close, and the choice of prior distributions will affect the estimates; in some applications that means one needs to think more carefully about those priors.
>
> In order to be able to identify the parameters consistently in a model with observation noise, one would at least need multiple realisations of the random field (which for some applications is fundamentally impossible).
>
> Finn
>
> > On 3 Jan 2022, at 18:55, 何博文 <steven...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > ﻿
> > Hi,
> >
> > My question is whether it is meaningful to use the INLA() function to estimate the underlying model parameters from a single realization that is generated by those model parameters to show that the INLA() function has the ability to reveal the true data-generating parameters. Since I was told that the parameters might not be consistently estimable given one single realization, I am wondering what is the purpose of the SPDE-toy example in the SPDE book and what is the takeaway of this example shown in the book?
> >
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Bowen

> > > One way to go is to fix one of the parameters, if you don't have both, infill and increased domain. In the spde-book we always fixed the smoothness parameter and considered increased domain for the simulated examples in order to be able to fit the other parameters.

> > > >
> > > > As I am doing the simulation study, I am curious that is the INLA() function cannot estimate model parameters consistenly under any scenarios or I can have certain confidence in believing some of the model scenarios such as the SPDEtoy exmaple? For instance, the SPDE toy in the book exhibits that the INLA() can successfully reveal the underlying true model parameters (including the covariance model parameters as well as the gaussian variances/nugget variances) from a single simple realisation. Is that mean in this model scenarios, the model parameters might not be consistenly estimable when changing the model parameters from only one model realization? What is the true purpose of this SPDE toy example when the parameters might not be consistently estimable from single realization that is sampled from some known model parameters? Thanks again for your reply!

> > > > > > Thanks for your reply!
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I apologize for the miscommunications in the previous question. I summarized two experiments here:
> > > > > > (1)  A very simple model with nugget effects only (variance of the only driving noise process). The INLA() function can reveal the true/appropriate nugget variances value in both the original 100*100 grid's value as observations and the composite averaged 10*10 coarser areal values as observations. If the original 100*100 grids simulation values are input to the INLA() function as observations, true nugget variances sigma^2 can be revealed and if the 10*10 composite averaged areal values are input to the INLA() function as observations, 1/100 times the true sigma^2 that I chose for simulating the finer grids value can also be successfully revealed. This simple nugget effect variance-only model is consistently estimable when a single realization is available.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > (2) Matern random field involved spatial model. The INLA() function can reveal a good estimation for all the covariance parameters (marginal variance for the process, scale/range) associated with the Matern field as well as the nugget effect's variance value when only one realization is available only when the original 100*100 finer grids values are input as observational values in the function. If the composite averaged areal values like 10*10 composite averaged areal values are input to the function as observations, the INLA() cannot derive the supposed 1/100 times the finer scale nugget effect sigma^2 value but all the other Matern covariance parameters.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thus, I am wondering why the INLA() function can successfully derive all the model parameters including the true nugget effect variance when observing the finer resolution grids value. However, the function failed to derive the 1/100 times the finer resolution nugget effect variance (precision for the gaussian observation calculated in this case is very different from 1/100 times the original nugget effect variance for finer grids) when observing aggregated scale values but still capable of deriving a good estimate for all the other Matern covariance parameters? Thanks!

> > > > > > > So it sounds like your actually getting the appropriate estimate, if your nugget variance estimate on the aggregated scale is 1/100 times that on the fine scale.

When the 10*10 coarser areal values that are averaged from the original finer grids values are used as input as observational values in the function, the INLA() function can also derive good estimation for all the covariance parameters (marginal variance for the process, scale/range) associated with Matern field, however, the nugget effect's sigma is off from the expected one (1/100 times the fine resolution nugget variance). Thus, in the context of the areal interpolation process which is to derive the original model parameters from coarser averaged composite observations (lower resolution to predict higher resolution), the model seems still able to derive the covariance parameters for a reasonable precision but only lose the ability to derive the nugget variances (precision for the gaussian observations). I am wondering what could be the possible reason for the INLA() function to lose the ability to reveal the underlying true nugget variances only in the context of the areal interpolation process using a single realization. messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] unexpected intra-variant variances estimation in disaggregation spatial regression model using INLA()
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] unexpected intra-variant variances estimation in disaggregation spatial regression model using INLA()
messages.body_plain:
There is a recent paper with some new results on this matter https://rss.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/rssb.12472

On Sat, 12 Mar 2022 at 20:48, 何博文 <steven...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks for your explanation! From multiple infill asymptotics simulations (100 realizations), I found there is a strong correlation between the marginal variances and the kappa estimates of those posterior estimates for the spde representation of the Matern field model from those 100 realizations. Based on this, I have two questions:
>
> (1) Is it appropriate to derive a relationship between those two model parameters (marginal variance and kappa/range) from the simulation data and apply the derived relationship in the real-world data to improve the prediction accuracy in the real-world data scenario? If it is doable, is there a way to constrain the model parameters and apply the derived relationship between the parameters in the inla() model to improve the prediction accuracy in the real-world data scenario?
>
> (2) Or the correlation and the uncertainty estimates of the spde Matern model parameters will not affect the prediction performance of the model with single realization data no matter what constrain/relationship of the model parameters are applied in the model? Since our main goal in the real-world data is to predict the missing values with only one observation and not to estimate the underlying model parameters, this could be helpful. Thanks!!
>
>
> Bowen
> On Monday, January 3, 2022 at 1:15:12 PM UTC-6 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Like I explained before, this is a fundamental property of even the simplest Gaussian Matern random field model, and has very little specific to do with either inla or the spde representations for Matern fields. Even in the case of a directly observed field (I.e. with no observation noise), infill asymptotics aren’t enough to consistently estimate all the model parameters. The best one can hope for is that the parameter estimates are reasonable, and that the resulting field properties (e.g. spatial prediction/infill) produces appropriate results with appropriate uncertainty estimates. One reference about the non-consistency of parameter estimates is  https://www.jstor.org/stable/20441245
> > Non-consistency however doesn’t mean that the parameter estimates are _necessarily_ far from the true values. It just means that there is no guarantee that they will be close, and the choice of prior distributions will affect the estimates; in some applications that means one needs to think more carefully about those priors.
> >
> > In order to be able to identify the parameters consistently in a model with observation noise, one would at least need multiple realisations of the random field (which for some applications is fundamentally impossible).
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > > On 3 Jan 2022, at 18:55, 何博文 <steven...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > ﻿
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > My question is whether it is meaningful to use the INLA() function to estimate the underlying model parameters from a single realization that is generated by those model parameters to show that the INLA() function has the ability to reveal the true data-generating parameters. Since I was told that the parameters might not be consistently estimable given one single realization, I am wondering what is the purpose of the SPDE-toy example in the SPDE book and what is the takeaway of this example shown in the book?
> > >
> > >
> > > Thanks,
> > > Bowen
> > >
> > > On Monday, January 3, 2022 at 4:35:56 AM UTC-6 eliask...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > Hi,
> > > > One way to go is to fix one of the parameters, if you don't have both, infill and increased domain. In the spde-book we always fixed the smoothness parameter and considered increased domain for the simulated examples in order to be able to fit the other parameters.
> > > > Elias
> > > >
> > > > On Mon, 3 Jan 2022 at 07:50, 何博文 <steven...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Thanks for your reply!
> > > > >
> > > > > As I am doing the simulation study, I am curious that is the INLA() function cannot estimate model parameters consistenly under any scenarios or I can have certain confidence in believing some of the model scenarios such as the SPDEtoy exmaple? For instance, the SPDE toy in the book exhibits that the INLA() can successfully reveal the underlying true model parameters (including the covariance model parameters as well as the gaussian variances/nugget variances) from a single simple realisation. Is that mean in this model scenarios, the model parameters might not be consistenly estimable when changing the model parameters from only one model realization? What is the true purpose of this SPDE toy example when the parameters might not be consistently estimable from single realization that is sampled from some known model parameters? Thanks again for your reply!
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks,
> > > > > Bowen
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Monday, December 20, 2021 at 1:02:05 PM UTC-6 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > I explained some of the possible reasons in a previous reply; the parameters are not consistently estimable even under infill asymptotics and known nugget variance, so you should not expect the nugget variance estimate to be close to the true data-generating value, for any estimation method.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Finn
> > > > > >
> > > > > > > On 20 Dec 2021, at 18:29, 何博文 <steven...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ﻿
> > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thanks for your reply!
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I apologize for the miscommunications in the previous question. I summarized two experiments here:
> > > > > > > (1)  A very simple model with nugget effects only (variance of the only driving noise process). The INLA() function can reveal the true/appropriate nugget variances value in both the original 100*100 grid's value as observations and the composite averaged 10*10 coarser areal values as observations. If the original 100*100 grids simulation values are input to the INLA() function as observations, true nugget variances sigma^2 can be revealed and if the 10*10 composite averaged areal values are input to the INLA() function as observations, 1/100 times the true sigma^2 that I chose for simulating the finer grids value can also be successfully revealed. This simple nugget effect variance-only model is consistently estimable when a single realization is available.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > (2) Matern random field involved spatial model. The INLA() function can reveal a good estimation for all the covariance parameters (marginal variance for the process, scale/range) associated with the Matern field as well as the nugget effect's variance value when only one realization is available only when the original 100*100 finer grids values are input as observational values in the function. If the composite averaged areal values like 10*10 composite averaged areal values are input to the function as observations, the INLA() cannot derive the supposed 1/100 times the finer scale nugget effect sigma^2 value but all the other Matern covariance parameters.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thus, I am wondering why the INLA() function can successfully derive all the model parameters including the true nugget effect variance when observing the finer resolution grids value. However, the function failed to derive the 1/100 times the finer resolution nugget effect variance (precision for the gaussian observation calculated in this case is very different from 1/100 times the original nugget effect variance for finer grids) when observing aggregated scale values but still capable of deriving a good estimate for all the other Matern covariance parameters? Thanks!
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thanks,
> > > > > > > Bowen
> > > > > > > On Monday, December 20, 2021 at 2:11:16 AM UTC-6 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > From my previous answer:
> > > > > > > > “ If the nugget variance from the 100x100 grid is sigma^2, then the nugget variance on the 10x10averaged grid is sigma^2 / 100 (average of 100 independent iid variables).”
> > > > > > > > So it sounds like your actually getting the appropriate estimate, if your nugget variance estimate on the aggregated scale is 1/100 times that on the fine scale.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Finn
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On 20 Dec 2021, at 06:05, 何博文 <steven...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > ﻿
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Thank you so much for your explanation.
> > > > > > > > > Yes, it helps a lot to understand this phenomenon.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Another interesting thing I found that is INLA() function can derive a very good estimation for all the covariance parameters (marginal variance for the process, scale/range) associated with the Matern field as well as the nugget effect's sigma^2 value even one realization is available under the condition that the original 100*100 finer grids values are input as observational values in the function, not the 10*10 coarser areal observational values. When the 10*10 coarser areal values that are averaged from the original finer grids values are used as input as observational values in the function, the INLA() function can also derive good estimation for all the covariance parameters (marginal variance for the process, scale/range) associated with Matern field, however, the nugget effect's sigma is off from the expected one (1/100 times the fine resolution nugget variance). Thus, in the context of the areal interpolation process which is to derive the original model parameters from coarser averaged composite observations (lower resolution to predict higher resolution), the model seems still able to derive the covariance parameters for a reasonable precision but only lose the ability to derive the nugget variances (precision for the gaussian observations). I am wondering what could be the possible reason for the INLA() function to lose the ability to reveal the underlying true nugget variances only in the context of the areal interpolation process using a single realization. Your thoughts would be extremely helpful! Thanks!
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > > > > Bowen
> > > > > > > > > On Friday, December 17, 2021 at 7:50:25 PM UTC-6 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > It is extremely likely that the model simply isn't identifiable. Even a model with _only_ a Matern field and no nugget has non-identifiable covariance parameters (only the variance of the driving noise process is consistently estimable under infill asymptotics) when only a single realisation is available.  It is therefore quite possible that INLA has actually computed an accurate estimate of the true posterior distribution for the problem presented to it, and that that posterior distribution isn't as close to the true parameter values as one might want it to be.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Finn
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > On Fri, 17 Dec 2021 at 19:38, 何博文 <steven...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > Thanks so much! It is so nice that you have answered.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Yes, I did two interesting experiments. The first one is that I used an arbitrarily chosen simple normal nugget effect (N(0, sigma)) to generate one single 100*100 grid realization, without intercept and any covariates, just the nugget effect (N(0, sigma)). Then, I averaged those 100*100 grids to 10*10 coarser averaged areal value, use INLA() to function to fit those coarser 10*10 averaged areal values. Even for this one single realization, the precision for the gaussian observation is 1/100 times the sigma of the finer resolution (100*100) nugget variance that I arbitrarily chose in the first place. This is aligned with a perfect world without any spatial random fields or SPDE model or numerical representation involved.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > However, if I added a Matérn covariance spatial random field in the simulation model, plus a simple intercept and a simple normal nugget effect like above, and fit the model on the composite averaged observations. The INLA() function cannot give accurate precision for the observation value for the averaged coarser areal observations (very different from 1/100 times the fine resolution nugget variance, which is expected). Thus, I am wondering if it is caused by the interaction with the numerical representation of the spatial random field itself, since the INLA() function can derive a good estimation on the pure composite nugget effects without any spatial random fields involved. Looking forward to your reply!
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Thanks,
> > > > > > > > > > > Bowen
> > > > > > > > > > > On Thursday, December 2, 2021 at 8:31:44 AM UTC-6 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > there isn't enough information provided to know for sure. If the nugget variance from the 100x100 grid is sigma^2, then the nugget variance on the 10x10averaged grid is sigma^2 / 100 (average of 100 independent iid variables).
> > > > > > > > > > > > So in a perfect world your nugget variance estimate should be 1/100 times the fine resolution nugget variance.
> > > > > > > > > > > > In practice, it will likely differ from that due to interaction with the numerical representation of the random field itself, and due to non-identifiability of the covariance parameters (with only a single field realisation, the parameters are not fully identifiable).
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Finn
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > On Thu, 2 Dec 2021 at 05:08, 何博文 <steven...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > I used an intercept, a multivariate normal distribution with Matérn covariance function and a nugget effect sigmae to simulate a spatial autocorrelated 100*100 grids value as simulation data. Then, I averaged 100 grids to one polygon, resulting  10*10 polygons as coarser observations. The goal is to predict the 10000 underlying grids level data when only observing those coarser a100 real/polygon observations. While INLA() can reveal the kappa, marignal variances of the Matérn covariance function as well as the intercept with a reasonable accuracy, the nugget effect sigmae is way off from the true value. I am wondering what might be the reason that costs this issue?

Even in the case of a directly observed field (I.e. with no observation noise), infill asymptotics aren’t enough to consistently estimate all the model parameters. The best one can hope for is that the parameter estimates are reasonable, and that the resulting field properties (e.g. spatial prediction/infill) produces appropriate results with appropriate uncertainty estimates. One reference about the non-consistency of parameter estimates is  https://www.jstor.org/stable/20441245
> > > Non-consistency however doesn’t mean that the parameter estimates are _necessarily_ far from the true values. It just means that there is no guarantee that they will be close, and the choice of prior distributions will affect the estimates; in some applications that means one needs to think more carefully about those priors.
> > >
> > > In order to be able to identify the parameters consistently in a model with observation noise, one would at least need multiple realisations of the random field (which for some applications is fundamentally impossible).

messages.subject: Re: Interpretation of the INLA summary results for Bayesian Cox PH model
messages.subject_clean: Interpretation of the INLA summary results for Bayesian Cox PH model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

You can find a good explanation in the book Bayesian Regression Modeling with INLA (https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/mono/10.1201/9781351165761/bayesian-regression-modeling-inla-xiaofeng-wang-yuryan-yue-julian-faraway).

And yes, you have to exponentiate the model summary. The raw output gives the treatment effect e.g. 0.5 (mean)  with 95% credible interval (0.5, 0.6). To get the posterior hazard ratio and it's 95% credible interval you have to exponentiale both of these terms.

Best, Eva

jerrymi...@gmail.com schrieb am Freitag, 19. Juni 2020 um 21:56:57 UTC+2:
> Hello group,
> I wanted to get this clear. When implementing the Cox PH model using the survival package we exponentiate the results to get the hazards. Should we also exponentiate the mean and their Credible intervals by using exp((model$ summary.fixed)? or do we just interpret the summary(model)?
> thanks,
> Jerita

messages.subject: Mapping the Odds Ratios from INLA-SPDE
messages.subject_clean: Mapping the Odds Ratios from INLA-SPDE
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Sorry to ask this naive question - after implementing a spatial model using INLA-SPDE to predict prevalence at unsampled locations with a likelihood function specified as binomial. Just like the predicted prevalence, I was wondering if was possible to also derive and map the Odds Ratios from this model - is it sensible to exponentiate the estimates from res$summary.random$s$mean (as well as those from 0.0025 & 0.975quant)?

model.formula <- y ~ 0 + b0 + temp + prec + elev + popl + f(s, model = spde.model) # here!

ptm <- proc.time()
res <- inla(model.formula, family = "binomial", Ntrials = numtrials,
                                                control.family = list(link = "logit"),
                                                data = inla.stack.data(stack.full),
                                                control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1, A = inla.stack.A(stack.full)))
proc.time() - ptm

Thank you very much.
Anwar.

messages.subject: problem with libpardiso.so in inla binary install
messages.subject_clean: problem with libpardiso.so in inla binary install
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users

We are having an issue which seems to be caused by the incompatibility of the standard INLA package with Redhat based systems. The cluster we are running INLA on is based on the Centos 7 distribution. We first got the following message:

"/lib64/libm.so.6: version `GLIBC_x.xx' not found"

To try to fix it, we tried the binary version of INLA. Thereafter, the following message appeared:

 "/scratch/apps/gnu/R-4.1.1/lib64/R/library/INLA/bin/linux/64bit/inla.mkl: error while loading shared libraries: libpardiso.so: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory".

We were not going to use pardiso in this application due to new licensing issues, but it seems that even in this situation the package depends on this library.

Márcio Laurini

messages.subject: INLA version of survSplit
messages.subject_clean: INLA version of survSplit
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

Does anyone know if it is possible to implement survSplit in INLA. In my analysis, I want to split  the follow-up time into two e.g the time at age 6 and analyze each time period. In the first time period or analysis will include all individuals in the cohort and follow-up stops at age 6. In the second, follow-up starts at age 6.

In the survival package, I think this can be achieve with the survSplit function. I tried the following in INLA and got an error.

vet2 <- survSplit(Surv(time, status) ~., veteran, cut=c(60, 120), episode ="timegroup")
sinla.vet <- inla.surv(vet2$tstart,vet2$time, vet2$status)

messages.body_plain:
Dear Maria,
The problem is that the fitted mean length is different from the SPDE model length. The projection should be from something at the mesh nodes and this seems not to be the case. Please compare the cases in section 2.4.2 and 2.5.3 of the spde-book (https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/)
Elias

messages.body_plain:
Dear Maria,
Unfortunately your code is not reproducible and thus we can only guess why this error is happening. My guess, as Finn already mentioned, is that the posterior marginals for the linear predictor were not computed. You can ask inla() to compute it by adding by compute=TRUE in control.predictor along with return.marginals.predictor=TRUE in control.results. Thus, your code will look like this:
    inla(..., control.predictor=list(A=..., compute=TRUE), control.results(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE), ...)
Best regards,
Elias

messages.body_plain:
INLA_22.03.24 is there now with quite a few internal changes (especially
for data-rich models and 'experimental' mode), so it is slightly more
'testing' than usual. Please be aware.

There was a regression bug in INLA_22.02.16 using
control.inla=list(strategy="laplace") that is now fixed in
INLA_22.03.24. Sorry about that one. The version in 'stable',
INLA_22.03.16, is also affected by this issue, but will be updated asap
we know there are no issues with this version.

The internal calculations have changed slightly for output compuations
and merging of marginal densities, so the results will be tiny different
compared to earlier versions. The mode of the density is now most often
reported as NA unless its know, as its to expensive to compute if one
does not need it.

If there is anything, please email he...@r-inla.org

Best
H
--
Håvard Rue
hr...@r-inla.org

messages.subject: Fit a normal curve with inlabru?
messages.subject_clean: Fit a normal curve with inlabru?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Having successfully fitted some nonlinear models with inlabru, I'm testing to see if I  can use it to fit a normal distribution curve to data. So far without success - it doesn't seem able to estimate the sd. Here's some example code:

library(data.table)
meand=0    #Mean of the curve
sdd=1      #sd of the curve
h=1        #height of the peak
x=seq(-10,10,length=1000)
varsamp=0.01          #error variance
precision=1/varsamp
sdsamp=sqrt(varsamp)

inputdt=data.table(expand.grid(x=x,ind=seq(1:10)))
inputdt[,indref:=paste("I",x,ind,sep="_")]
inputdt[,h:=h]
inputdt[,meand:=meand]
inputdt[,sdd:=sdd]

#data points including error variance.
inputdt[,normcurve:=h*exp(-((x - meand)^2/(2*sdd^2))) + rnorm(.N,0,sdsamp)]

plot(normcurve~x,data=inputdt)
points((h*exp(-((x - meand)^2/(2*sdd^2))))~x,data=inputdt,col="red",pch=16,cex=0.3)

#Likelihood model.
  lik <- inlabru::like(
    family = "gaussian", data = inputdt,
    formula = normcurve~h*exp(-((x - meand)^2/(2*sdd^2)))
  )

#This doesn't work.
fita <- bru(~ h(1) + meand(1) + sdd(1) - 1, lik)
summary(fita)

#This works.
fita2 <- bru(~ h(1) + meand(1) - 1, lik)
summary(fita2)

I know I can use other packages for this, I'm actually fitting a more complex model, which also works well if I don't try to estimate the sdd parameter.

Is there a way to fit this model?

Thanks, Richard.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Fit a normal curve with inlabru?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Fit a normal curve with inlabru?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

it's an initial value issue; The default starting point for the
linearisation is all latent variables being zero. In your
parameterisation, there's no way to "escape" from that point.
You can set initial values for the two problematic parameters h and sdd with
  options = list(bru_initial = list(h = 2, sdd = 2))

However, that's not quite enough, as the parameterisation doesn't have
a unique solution for sdd; the predictor isn't monotonic in sdd.
But this is easily fixed here, since you can use a log-transformation
for the sdd parameterisation, with exp(log_sdd) instead of sdd.
The following works:

lik <- inlabru::like(
  family = "gaussian", data = inputdt,

  formula = normcurve~h*exp(-((x - meand)^2/(2*exp(log_sdd)^2)))
)
fita <- bru(~ h(1) + meand(1) + log_sdd(1) - 1, lik,
            options = list(bru_initial = list(h = 2)))

> fita$summary.fixed
                mean          sd   0.025quant     0.5quant
0.975quant mode          kld
h        1.010092214 0.004245507  1.001768795  1.010092215
1.018415635   NA 5.543583e-11
meand    0.001966013 0.004772272 -0.007390147  0.001966014
0.011322175   NA 5.353491e-11
log_sdd -0.010752056 0.004821584 -0.020204893 -0.010752055
-0.001299217   NA 5.352113e-11
> exp(fita$summary.fixed["log_sdd", c("0.025quant", "0.5quant", "0.975quant")])
        0.025quant  0.5quant 0.975quant
log_sdd  0.9799979 0.9893055  0.9987016

Finn

messages.subject: Extrapolation of rw1 effects
messages.subject_clean: Extrapolation of rw1 effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I'm trying to make models with some non-linear effects, aiming to make predictions of species occurrence in future scenarios. I'm using random walks of order 1, as in this work https://arxiv.org/pdf/1708.03156.pdf (and considering https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-smoothing.html). However, I'm not sure of how these random effects behavior when exposed to new data out of the original range (i.e. extrapolating). In my models I'm getting a linear extrapolation, don't matter how is the tendency of the smoothed curve.

See this example of a binomial model and plot attached:

# set a dummy dataset
library(INLA)
set.seed(2000)

bvar <- dnorm(1:100, mean = 50, sd = 10)
binom <- data.frame(
        var = 1:70,
        resp = rbinom(70, 1, (bvar-min(bvar))/(max(bvar)-min(bvar)))
)

# Run the binomial model
binom.model <- inla(resp ~ f(inla.group(var, n = 20), model = "rw1"),
                    family = "binomial", Ntrials = 2, data = binom)

# Plot effects
ylim <- c(min(c(binom.model$summary.random[[1]]$`0.025quant`)),
          max(c(binom.model$summary.random[[1]]$`0.975quant`)))
plot(c(binom.model$summary.random[[1]]$mean) ~
             binom.model$summary.random[[1]]$ID, type = "l",
     main = "var", ylim = ylim,
     xlab = "", ylab = "Effect")
abline(h = 0, lty = "dashed", lwd = 1, col = "gray70")
lines(x=binom.model$summary.random[[1]]$ID,
      y=c(binom.model$summary.random[[1]]$`0.025quant`),
      lwd=2, lty="dashed", col="blue")
lines(x=binom.model$summary.random[[1]]$ID,
      y=c(binom.model$summary.random[[1]]$`0.975quant`),
      lwd=2, lty="dashed", col="blue")

# Predict to a new range
pred.data <- rbind(binom,
                   cbind(var = 70:150,
                         resp = NA))

pred.model <- inla(resp ~ f(inla.group(var, n = 20), model = "rw1"),
                   family = "binomial", Ntrials = 2, data = pred.data)

# Plot predictions
ylim <- c(min(c(pred.model$summary.random[[1]]$`0.025quant`)),
          max(c(pred.model$summary.random[[1]]$`0.975quant`)))
plot(c(pred.model$summary.random[[1]]$mean) ~
             pred.model$summary.random[[1]]$ID, type = "l",
     main = "var", ylim = ylim,
     xlab = "", ylab = "Effect")
abline(h = 0, lty = "dashed", lwd = 1, col = "gray70")
abline(v = 70, lty = "dashed", lwd = 1, col = "red")
text(x = 92, y = 2, labels = "> Extrapolation", col = "red")
lines(x=pred.model$summary.random[[1]]$ID,
      y=c(pred.model$summary.random[[1]]$`0.025quant`),
      lwd=2, lty="dashed", col="blue")
lines(x=pred.model$summary.random[[1]]$ID,
      y=c(pred.model$summary.random[[1]]$`0.975quant`),
      lwd=2, lty="dashed", col="blue")

Is there anything that I can do to make the model to extrapolate following the curve tendency? Or is there an alternative to rw1 to fit non-linear effects?

Thanks in advance!

(just a note: my case is study is far more complex than this example, and includes an SPDE for the spatial component)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Extrapolation of rw1 effects
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Extrapolation of rw1 effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The conditional expectation of a RW(1) model beyond the data range is constant, which is what you got.  For a RW(2) model, extrapolations are straight lines.
The first order random walk pulls the first order differences towards zero, so where there is no observations to say otherwise, the expectation gets pulled to a function with zero derivative, I.e. a constant.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
The rw2 model is associated with regular cubic splines, via the int (f’k(t))^2 dt penalty.
You can also use 1d Matern proper covariance models, via 1d mesh models and inla.spde2.pcmatern.
The extrapolation behaviour of rw1 models is inherent in that model choice, so if you need other extrapolation behaviour you need to change your model.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
In the bayesian setting with Gaussian priors on the coefficients, splines are just special cases of Gaussian processes. In particular penalized splines; when you have enough basis functions/knots, a proper penalty yields a well defined continuous time/space Gaussian process.

Finn
